# Hirocidins, Cytotoxic Metabolites from Streptomyces hiroshimensis, Induce Mitochondrion-Mediated Apoptosis

**Authors:** Esther J. Han; Myungeun Jeong; Seoung Rak Lee; Erik J. Sorensen; Mohammad R. Seyedsayamdost

**Affiliations:** Departments of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 (USA) | Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 (USA) | College of Pharmacy, Pusan National University, Busan 46241 (South Korea) | Department of Chemistry, Princeton University Princeton, NJ 08544 (USA); Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University Princeton, NJ 08544 (USA)

## Abstract

Recent advances in whole genome sequencing have revealed an immense microbial potential for the production of therapeutic small molecules, even from well-known producers. To access this potential, we subjected prominent antimicrobial producers to alternative antiproliferative assays using persistent cancer cell lines. Described herein is our discovery of hirocidins, novel secondary metabolites from Streptomyces hiroshimensis with antiproliferative activities against colon and persistent breast cancer cells. Hirocidin A is an unusual nine-membered carbocyclic maleimide and hirocidins B and C are relatives with an unprecedented, bridged azamacrocyclic backbone. Mode of action studies show that hirocidins trigger mitochondrion-dependent apoptosis by inducing expression of the key apoptotic effector caspase-9. The discovery of new cytotoxins contributes to scaffold diversification in anticancer drug discovery and the reported modes of action and concise total synthetic route for variant A set the stage for unraveling specific targets and biochemical interactions of the hirocidins.

## Introduction

Owing to millions of years of evolution, natural products have emerged with wide-ranging physiological functions and inspired chemists and biologists alike with their complex structures and therapeutic activities.[1,2] Actinomycete bacteria, in particular, have offered an unparalleled source of antimicrobial and anticancer agents with vancomycin and mitomycin providing but two well-known examples of such therapeutics.[3,4] Recent advances in DNA sequencing technologies coupled with bioinformatics indicate that the natural products discovered so far merely represent the tip of the iceberg as the products of most biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) that can be observed in microbial genomes remain to be identified.[5,6] Even microbes previously considered exhausted or ‘drained’ have emerged as valuable reservoirs of untapped metabolites and, with the appropriate discovery methods, these strains can yield new and potentially useful compounds.[7–9]

Motivated by this untapped potential and the possibility of finding new molecules from well-studied strains, we subjected established antimicrobial producers to antiproliferative assays against persistent cancer cell lines. We discovered five novel natural products including hirocidins A-C that form a new chemotype and are constitutively produced by Streptomyces hiroshimensis. Hirocidin A possesses a carbocyclic maleimide; its structure was established by spectroscopic analysis as well as a concise total synthesis route. Variants B and C contain a bridged azaheterocyclic backbone within a larger macrocyle. Hirocidins display promising cytotoxic activities and subsequent mode of action studies showed that they induce cell death by caspase-9-mediated apoptosis. Our work is in line with the notion that even well-trodden strains remain useful sources of new natural products. The discovery and total synthesis of hirocidin A will facilitate structure activity relationships to better understand and enhance its anticancer activity.

## Results and Discussion

### Identification of Antiproliferative Activities in S. hiroshimensis

We subjected three well-studied streptomycetes that are known for their antimicrobial arsenal to colorimetric antiproliferative assays: Streptomyces griseus, the producer of streptomycin,[10] Streptomyces clavuligerus, the source of clavulanic acid,[11] and S. hiroshimensis, which generates several products including the Gram-negative selective taylorflavin antibiotics.[12] Cell-free supernatants from each strain were concentrated 2.5-fold and then tested against HCT116 colon cancer cells using the 3-(4,5-diemthylthiazol-2-yl)-5-(3-carboxymethoxyphenyl)-2-(4-sulfophe-nyl)-2H-tetrazolium (MTS) viability assay as read-out. We observed minimal growth inhibition from extracts of S. griseus and S. clavuligerus (Figure 1A). S. hiroshimensis extracts, however, exhibited significant antiproliferative activity, resulting in 98.1% growth inhibition compared to vehicle control. The majority of this effect could be attributed to metabolites derived from cell pellets, which are often ignored in drug discovery campaigns (Figure 1B).

### Characterization of Cell Pellet-Associated Cytotoxins

Bioassay-guided fractionation from S. hiroshimensis pellets in conjunction with HPLC-MS-based dereplication pointed to six metabolites with varying degrees of cytotoxicity (Figure 1C, Table S1). Of these, four did not return any matches in natural product databases,[13] which we prioritized for further study. The strongest antiproliferative activity was associated with compound 1, which we have termed hirocidin A. 1D NMR spectra and COSY correlations suggested a substituted nine-membered carbocycle fused to an olefinic ring (Figure S1, Table S2). HMBC and HSQC correlations in combination with chemical shift analysis revealed a maleimide with key cross-peaks from H-1 to C-10a/C-10 as well as from H-7 to C-7a/C-8, thus completing the planar structure of 1, consistent with the molecular formula of C15H23NO2 derived from HR-MS analysis. The stereogenic center at C-7 was determined to be R-configured using electronic circular dichroism (ECD) calculations and CD spectroscopy (Figure S2, Tables S3 and S4).[14] Hirocidin A is a novel natural product with an unusual maleimide, a substructure that has been observed only in a few instances, including the nucleoside antibiotic showdomycin and the fungus-derived cytotoxin oxalamide I.[15–20]

We next focused on compounds 2 and 3, which based on initial analysis, were in a diastereomeric relationship with a molecular formula of C25H32N2O4 (Table S1). The presence of nine-membered carbocycles with an n-butyl side chain was deduced, similarly to the case of 1, from COSY and HMBC correlations (Figures S3 and S4, Table S5). Further analysis of 1D/2D NMR spectra showed that both compounds possess a structurally unprecedented architecture consisting of a pyrrole-fused and amide-bridged azecinedione backbone. Key HMBC correlations from H-1 to C-17, H-9 to C-7a/C-11, as well as NOESY cross-peaks emanating from H-9 to H-1’/H-12, among others, allowed us to deduce the presence of the azaheterocyclic framework with three carbonyl groups at C-10 (201.0 ppm), C-17 (165.3 ppm), and C-18 (183.4 ppm). Collectively, these and other spectral data completed the planar structures of 2 (hirocidin B) and 3 (hirocidin C).

The analogous 13C NMR shifts and minimal changes in 1H NMR resonances at C-7 of 2 and 3, relative to 1, suggested an R configuration (Tables S2 and S5). The absolute configuration of C-11 was determined by subjecting all four diastereomers to ECD calculations (Figure S5, Tables S6–S9). Experimental CD spectra indicated that 2 and 3 contain the (7R, 11R) and (7R, 11S) configurations, respectively. GIAO-based NMR calculations and DP4 probability analysis were consistent with these assignments (Figures S6 and S7, Table S10),[14,21] thus completing the structures of these two novel metabolites, which form a new chemotype owing to the bridged azamacrocyclic moiety and an unusual arrangement of two azaheterocycles within a larger macrocycle.

The final new metabolite from S. hiroshimensis cell pellets, compound 4 termed taylorflavin C, was also characterized spectroscopically. 1D/2D NMR data showed 4 as a new congener of the taylorflavins. Compared to taylorflavin B, 4 has an additional pyrrole and methoxy functional group attached to the 2-methylfervenulone backbone at N-1 and N-4, respectively,[12] as evidenced by a NOESY cross-peak between H-4’ and N-2-Me, along with other correlations (Figures S8 and S9, Table S11). Indeed, production of 4 was abrogated in a taylorflavin gene deletion mutant (toxB-tflA::apr, Figure S10). The two remaining metabolites, compounds 5 and 6 with vibrant red pigmentation, were identified as undecylprodigiosin and streptorubin B using MS-based dereplication and NMR analysis (Figure S11, Table S1),[22–25] thus completing the identification of cytotoxic products from S. hiroshimensis cell pellets.

### Characterization of Culture Supernatant-Associated Cytotoxins

We also pursued the moderate activities observed from the supernatant. Activity-guided fractionation led to compound 7 with a molecular formula of C16H19NO4 as determined by HR-MS (Figure 1D, Table S1). 1D/2D NMR spectra revealed a 1,7-dimethoxynaphthalene moiety substituted with a 3-hydroxy-butanamide fragment based on HMBC cross-peaks from H-1’ to C-2, C-3, and C-4 (Figure S12, Table S11). Attempts to assign the absolute configuration at C-2’ by Mosher’s analysis failed possibly due to hydrogen bonding between C-2’-OH and the terminal amide at C-4’. Thus, we resorted to ECD studies, which suggested an S-configuration at the secondary alcohol (Figure S13, Tables S12 and S13). Compound 7, termed hironaphthamide, is a novel metabolite notable for its naphthalene framework and the unusual 3-hydroxybutanamide moiety. Seven additional metabolites (compounds 8–14, Figure S14) were isolated by following antiproliferative activities and MS-based dereplication, revealing the previously reported natural products pyrizinostatin (8), BE-54238A and B (9 and 10), which we showed are synthesized by the hiroshidine BGC (Figure S10), 3-methyllumichrome (11), and three isocoumarin derivatives (12–14).[12,26–33] Pyrizinostatin and BE-54238A/B were originally isolated from Streptomyces sp. SA-2289 and Streptomyces sp. A54238, respectively, while 3-methyllumichrome and the isocoumarin derivatives have been reported from several actinomycetes, including Strepomyces sp. MBT76. Compounds 8–13 are new to S. hiroshimensis.

### IC50 Analysis of Isolated Metabolites

With pure metabolites at hand, we quantified their antiproliferative properties against HCT116 colon cancer cells, MDA-MB-231 persistent metastatic breast cancer cells, as well as the control cell line RPE-1 (retinal pigment epithelial cells, Table 1). Compounds 1–3 with the novel chemotypes exhibited cytotoxic activities with half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50s) ranging from 1.7 to 23 μg/mL. Consistent with recent results with prodigiosin,[22,34,35] we observed potent anticancer activities of 5 and 6 with IC50s between 0.002–0.37 μg/mL. All five metabolites were less effective against RPE-1 cells, displaying a small degree of selectivity. As expected, metabolites from S. hiroshimensis supernatants did not show strong inhibitory activities.

### Hirocidins, Potent Inducers of Mitochondrion-Mediated Apoptosis

Given the potent activities and new scaffolds of 1–3, we set out to investigate their modes of action. Anticancer agents typically act through four pathways (Figure 2A).[36–38] We treated HCT116 cells with 5 μg/mL 1 or 25 μg/mL 2 (~3-fold IC50) and assessed the expression of 3–5 genes within (i) the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling circuit, (ii) the p53 pathway, and (iii) the extrinsic apoptotic pathway,[36–38] but found no significant effects (Figures 2A and S15). To probe (iv) the mitochondrion-dependent intrinsic apoptotic pathway, we first assessed the mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) upon exposure to hirocidins using JC-1, a cationic carbocyanine dye that is selectively retained in intact mitochondrial membranes and shows potential-dependent fluorescence. Unlike vehicle control, which exhibited strong red fluorescence as a result of MMP-dependent aggregation of JC-1 in mitochondria, treatment with 1 or 2 led to higher green fluorescence associated with JC-1 monomers, indicating a loss of the MMP and a subsequent redistribution of JC-1 from mitochondria into the cytoplasm, analogous to the phenotype observed with the well-known anticancer agent etoposide (Figure 2B). Quantitative fluorescence spectroscopic analysis revealed 53%, 66%, and 58% reduction in the ratio of red to green fluorescence upon treatment with 1, 2, or etoposide, respectively (Figure 2C), indicating that MMP disruption is a key consequence of hirocidin treatment.

To gain further insights, we examined key genes involved in the intrinsic apoptotic pathway in response to 1 (Figure 3A),[39–41] and found significantly enhanced expression of caspase-9, an important apoptotic effector involved in abnormal cellular proliferation and oxidative stress, as well as poly-ADP ribose polymerase (PARP), a major enzymatic component of DNA damage repair (Figure 3B).[39–41] Hirocidin B treatment only led to induction of caspase-9, perhaps indicative of its weaker antiproliferative activity (Figure 3C). To further verify that hirocidins act through the apoptotic pathway, we tested the transcriptional response in caspase-9 knockdown cells prepared via short interfering ribonucleic acids (siRNA) and observed reduced transcription of caspase-3 and PARP in the presence of 1 (Figures 3D and S16). Moreover, wild-type HCT116 cells treated with the specific caspase-9 inhibitor Ac-LEHD-CMK (10 μM) showed 2.5- or 6.5-fold greater tolerance to 1 and 2, respectively (Figures 3E and S17). The anticancer drugs etoposide and cisplatin reduce tumor growth by triggering intrinsic apoptosis.[40–42] Collectively, our results indicate that hirocidins act through the same pathway and trigger HCT116 cell death via mitochondrial damage, activation of caspase-9, and subsequent initiation of intrinsic apoptosis (Figure 3A). These results pave the way for more detailed mode-of-action studies in the future.

### Chemical Synthesis of Hirocidin A

Among the five newly discovered compounds, hirocidin A is especially interesting due to its antiproliferative properties and structural simplicity. We established a concise laboratory synthesis of 1 by the sequence of reactions shown in Scheme 1 to confirm our structural assignment and set the stage for future structure–activity relationship investigations. The combined action of ethyl diazoacetate and boron trifluoride etherate on commercially available cyclooctanone (15) caused a needed ring expansion[43] and the formation of 2-carbethoxycyclononanone (16) as a 5:4 mixture of keto/enol tautomers (Figure S18). An α-selenation of 16 was followed by oxidative deselenation to give α,β-unsaturated keto ester 17 (Figure S19). Introduction of the butyl chain in the course of a Cu(II)-catalyzed 1,4-conjugate addition of di-n-butyl zinc to 17 afforded 18[44,45] and was followed by an efficient base-mediated formation of vinyltriflate 19 (Figures S20 and S21). While methoxycarbonylations of 19 were successful, we were unable to advance the resulting substituted maleate diester to 1. On the other hand, the nitrile group of 20, the product of a Pd(0)-catalyzed cyanation of 19 with Zn(II) cyanide,[46] underwent a hydration in the presence of Parkins’ catalyst[47] and a spontaneous cyclization[48] to yield racemic 1 (Figures S22–S24). This racemic mixture was successfully resolved, allowing us to identify the enantiomer that had identical chromatographic properties with authentic 1. The spectroscopic data for synthetic and authentic hirocidin A showed excellent agreement and their IC50 traces are highly analogous (Figures S25–S27). The synthesis outlined in Scheme 1 offers opportunities for generating an expanded family of hirocidin A congeners and exploring the structural features that are critical for cytotoxic activity.

## Conclusion

Advances in genome sequencing and bioinformatics indicate that the natural products characterized thus far represent but a small fraction of biosynthetic potential encoded in microbial genomes and that the products of many orphan BGCs remain to be mapped. In this study, we utilized one of the simplest approaches for natural product discovery and focused on streptomycete strains that were previoulsy mined for antibiotics. Using S. hiroshimensis, a decades-old model strain, we uncovered otherwise undetectable metabolites using MTS-based cytotoxicity assays, in line with the notion that well-known microbial strains still harbor hidden bioactive molecules waiting to be uncovered.

Hirocidins stand out for their promising antiproliferative activities and novel chemotype. Variants B and C offer further avenues for biosynthetic investigations as the introduction of azaheterocycles within a larger macrocycle is intriguing. In addition, hirocidin A, the most active of the three, provides opportunities to better understand and enhance its toxicity toward cancer cell lines. Cyclic imides such as thalidomide and amidosuccinimide have recently been identified as substrates for cereblon (CRBN), an essential component of the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, which facilitates targeted protein degradation.[49,50] Hirocidin A contains the key cyclic imide moiety. However, maleimides exhibit weaker CRBN binding than succinimides. Moreover, the phthalimide carbonyl group of thalidomide is important for the interaction as it forms a hydrogen bond with the conserved Asn50 of CRBN.[51,52] These differences explain why 1 is unlikely to bind CRBN and display immunomodulatory effects, as borne out by the mechanism of action studies, which instead point to apoptosis via a mitochondrion-mediated pathway. Whether 1 plays additional biological roles remains to be determined. Hirocidin A offers an ideal candidate for structural diversification by the methods of organic synthesis given its simple molecular structure; this approach can be leveraged in an effort to conduct further mechanistic studies and discover new congeners with improved therapeutic potential.[53]

# Homo-Clavulyne: Evaluation of a One-Atom Ring Expansion Strategy to Stabilize the Nine-Membered Ring Enediyne Biosynthetic Precursor

**Authors:** Lande Hu; Myungeun Jeong; Mohammad R Seyedsayamdost; Erik J Sorensen

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, United States

## Abstract

Streptomyces clavuligerus biosynthesizes a nine-membered ring enediyne that spontaneously cycloaromatizes to a 1,4-benzenoid diradical enroute to the clavulynes. Since nature also produces several isolable and exceedingly cytotoxic metabolites featuring 10-membered ring enediynes, we reasoned that a ring-expanded “homo-clavulyne” enediyne might be accessible by the concepts and methods of organic synthesis, isolable, and useful as a new molecular warhead with therapeutic applications. The design of a 10-membered ring homo-clavulyne enediyne and our circumstantial evidence for its existence are described herein.

Keywords: clavulynes, homo-clavulyne enediyne, Bergman cycloaromatization, Sonogashira coupling, Kobayashi borylation, Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi cyclization

## Abstract

## Introduction

When the Bergman laboratory presented chemical evidence for the intermediacy of 1,4-benzenoid diradicals in thermal isomerizations of cis-1,5-diyn-3-enes (Fig. 1),1 the chemical community was unaware that nature had already evolved a family of exceedingly cytotoxic natural products that harness this chemistry to effect cleavages of double-stranded DNA and cell death. The same type of conjugated six-carbon unit at the heart of Bergman’s pioneering studies is also a prominent structural element in calicheamicin γI,2 esperamicin,3 dynemicin A,4 maduropeptin,5 and other natural products (not shown)6 that bind to DNA and may be triggered to undergo analogous cycloaromatizations to a 1,4-benzene diradical capable of abstracting hydrogen atoms from the phosphate backbone of DNA. Neocarzinostatin is structurally distinct from these aforementioned natural products but can be induced to undergo an analogous Myers–Saito cyclization to a lethal diradical that also abstracts hydrogen atoms from DNA and triggers apoptosis.7 These discoveries were captivating and stimulated a great deal of research in the area of organic synthesis, with a particular focus on the context dependence of Bergman cycloaromatization chemistry, for example, correlations between molecular strain and c–d distances with proclivities toward cycloaromatization,8 and the therapeutic potential of the enediyne antitumor antibiotics and novel compounds derived from them (e.g., Mylotarg).9

*Fig. 1: The Bergman cycloaromatization and the structures of selected members of the enediyne class of antitumor natural products.*

Some members of this unique class of natural products, for example, sporolides A and B,10 the cyanonsporasides,11 fijiolide B,12 the amycolamycins,13 and the clavulynes,14 originate from enediyne precursors that are too unstable to be isolated.15 The clavulynes, recently described by Seyedsayamdost and coworkers,14 are cryptic enediyne-derived metabolites produced by Streptomyces clavuligerus. These metabolites arise from a fleeting nine-membered ring enediyne 1 (Scheme 1a) that cannot be isolated in laboratory settings. The assumption is that S. clavuligerus biosynthesizes the pre-clavulyne enediyne 1 for offensive purposes and that this reactive, unstable compound undergoes a spontaneous Bergman cyclization to a cytotoxic 1,4-benzenoid diradical (2), giving rise to clavulyne E (3) by hydrogen atom transfers to the diradical and the related monohalogenated clavulynes by the Perrin–O’Connor reaction.16

*Scheme 1: (a) The putative nine-membered ring pre-clavulyne enediyne (1), cytotoxic 1,4-benzenoid diradical (2) and clavulyne E (3). (b) The structures of enantiomeric 10-membered ring homo-clavulyne enediynes 4 and 5, and our synthetic strategy.*

To date, there are at least eight structurally distinct natural products with the enediyne array confined to an isolable and relatively stable 10 membered ring. On this basis, we hypothesized that a 10-membered ring ‘homo-clavulyne’ enediyne (e.g., 4 and 5, Scheme 1b) might be accessible by organic synthesis and possibly also isolable and therapeutically useful. A one-atom extension may seem to be a minor structural modification, yet numerous examples have demonstrated that a difference of a single atom can induce substantial changes in chemical and biological properties.17 The testing of this hypothesis and our initial effort to stabilize the fugitive pre-clavulyne enediyne by a one-atom ring expansion are described herein.

At the outset, our thinking was influenced by the broad applicability of the Sonogashira cross-coupling method18 to the problem of constructing enediyne arrays, as well as by the successful cyclizations that the groups of Kende,19 Danishefsky,20 and Nicolaou21 had achieved in their syntheses of the challenging molecular architecture of calicheamicin γI. In principle, the 10-membered rings in homo-clavulynes 4 and 5 could arise by a strategy comprising a convergent Sonogashira coupling (e.g., between alkyne 6 and vinyl bromide 7) and some type of intramolecular addition of an alkyne-based nucleophile to a carbonyl group. These potential bond constructions seemed reasonable and yet the highly substituted cyclopentene 6, with its three contiguous oxygen-bearing stereocenters, would still be challenging to synthesize in a concise fashion. As matters transpired, we evaluated three distinct pathways for synthesizing compound 6 (Supporting Information) before settling on an approach featuring a 1,4-borylation/oxidation. During this undertaking, ent-homo-clavulyne 5 became our preferred target for synthesis only because we detected a stereochemical correspondence between key intermediate 6 and a known derivative of D-ribose. We also knew that a successful synthesis of 5 could be easily adapted to a synthesis of the enantiomeric homo-clavulyne 4 if desired.

In fact, D-ribose derivative 8 (Scheme 2a) is commercially available, relatively inexpensive, and possesses a cis-fused bicyclic framework that could be leveraged to control the stereochemical outcome of the eventual 1,4-borylation (vide infra). α-Iodination of cyclopentenone 8 afforded iodoenone 9 in 86% yield and was followed by standard Sonogashira coupling with trimethylsilylacetylene to give the alkynyl enone 10 in 82% yield.18 The two-carbon extension of the carbonyl group in 10 presented the first challenge in our synthesis. Several methods, including Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons, Peterson olefination, and aldol addition with lithio ethyl acetate followed by β-hydroxy elimination, failed to furnish the desired ester 11. To our delight, a Wittig olefination using stabilized phosphorane 12 in refluxing toluene afforded 11 in 69% yield.

At this stage, we needed to achieve a site- and stereoselective hydration of the newly constructed electron-deficient alkene and were drawn to the effective copper-catalyzed method developed by the Kobayashi laboratory.22 When catalyzed by a chiral CuII-bis (hydroxymethyl)bipyridyl complex, Kobayashi’s β-selective hydration of 1,6-unsaturated carbonyls is enantio-selective and performs well on a range of 1,6-unsaturated carbonyl substrates.22 Since the rigid, cis-fused bicyclic structure of 11 was expected to impart substantial facial selectivity, the achiral bis(hydroxymethyl)bipyridyl ligand (L) was employed for this reaction. Following reaction optimization (Supporting Information), we were pleased to find that the CuII-catalyzed 1,4-borylation of compound 11 in degassed, wet tetrahydrofuran (THF) under exclusion of light, followed by in situ oxidation of the resulting organoborane, produced alcohol 13 in 65% yield on a gram scale. To set the stage for the key Sonogashira cross-coupling, compound 13 was converted to terminal alkyne 14 via compound 6 by the two-step reaction sequence shown. Notably, trimethylsilyl deprotection of the alkyne in 13 with tetra-n-butyl-ammonium fluoride resulted in decomposition in absence of acetic acid, possibly due to the degradation of the β-hydroxy functionality through retro-aldol or E1cB elimination under basic conditions. To suppress this degradation pathway in subsequent transformations, the alcohol was protected as the corresponding tert-butyldimethylsilyl ether to afford 14 as the alkyne coupling fragment. We had hoped that vinyl bromide 7, bearing a pendant ethenyl group, could serve as a suitable coupling partner for the Sonogashira reaction (Scheme 2b). Unfortunately, however, the outcome we observed suggests that the initially formed organopalladium(II) intermediate 15 isomerizes to 17 prior to transmetalation and this isomerization is thermodynamically favored (Supporting Information). Consequently, vinyl bromide 18b was prepared in one step from the known alcohol 18a as an alternative coupling fragment,23 equipped with a protected alcohol as a useful functional group handle.

While coupling partners 14 and 18 were in hand, the pivotal Sonogashira reaction required extensive screening to find the most optimal conditions (Supporting Information). Ultimately, we found that conducting this coupling in strictly degassed, anhydrous DMF with exclusion of light and in presence of dual base additives minimizes substrate decomposition and undesired Glaser homocoupling, affording enediyne 19 in 74% yield. In the wake of this fragment coupling, the silyl-protected alkyne was converted to the corresponding iodoalkyne 20a and also the terminal alkyne 20b using AgNO3 catalysis in preparation for the efforts to construct the desired homo-clavulyne 10-membered ring.24,25

The two options we favored for achieving ring formation required the seemingly straightforward conversion of the ethyl esters in compounds 20a and 20b to aldehydes. We first attempted the complete reductions of the esters in 20a/20b to primary alcohols, followed by a separate step of Dess–Martin oxidation to acquire the corresponding aldehydes. However, the resulting aldehydes underwent rapid decomposition during column chromatography on silica, deactivated silica, alumina, or Florisil, presumably via facile E1cB eliminations of the β-silyloxy substituents and secondary degradation pathways. Unfortunately, all other efforts, including Piancatelli–Margarita, Stahl, Parikh–Doering, Albright–Goldman, Ley–Griffith, Swern, and Fétizon oxidations, failed to produce the desired aldehydes (Supporting Information). Ultimately, we found that diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL-H) mediated partial reductions of esters 20a and 20b were successful at −78 °C and afforded the sensitive aldehydes 21a and 21b, respectively, as stable, isolable compounds after a Fieser workup of the reactions (Scheme 3).26 In this fashion, the desired aldehydes were produced cleanly with no sign of unreacted starting material and only trace amounts of overreduction products.

With the desired cyclization substrates finally in hand, a one-carbon homologue of the putative pre-clavulyne enediyne 1 was nearly within reach. Could we generate a homo-clavulyne framework in the course of an intramolecular carbonyl addition and would the resulting adduct be isolable and relatively stable? We examined several methods for generating acetylide nucleophiles from 21a or 21b (Supporting Information). Deprotonation of the alkynyl hydrogen on 21b with potassium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide or tBuLi resulted in full decomposition of the aldehyde likely due to the competing deprotonation of the α-hydrogens. Carreira’s mild conditions for generating ZnII-acetylides using stoichiometric Zn(OTf)2 and NEt3 also led to decomposition of the aldehyde,27 presumably for the same reason. Eventually, we found that a Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi reaction28 on substrate 21a using catalytic NiCl2 and a large excess of CrCl2 in strictly deoxygenated and anhydrous THF generated a putative CrIII-acetylide that added intramolecularly to the aldehyde. We hoped and even expected to isolate 10-membered ring enediyne 23 from this reaction but could infer only that this compound formed as a transient intermediate enroute to the cycloaromatized product 25, which we isolated after workup of the reaction. Compound 23 (or its alkoxide precursor 22) underwent a premature Bergman cycloaromatization and the resulting benzenoid diradical 24 abstracted hydrogen atoms, presumably from THF, leading to the polycyclic benzene 25 as a 1:1 mixture of benzylic alcohol epimers. These inseparable epimers were isolated together in an overall yield of 50% from iodoalkyne ester 20a, while the remaining of the mass balance was attributed to 21b via inefficient acetylide addition and uncontrolled radical degradation.

The clavulynes are cryptic gene products that originate from a putative, unstable nine-membered ring enediyne. Since nature also biosynthesizes several 10-membered ring enediynes that may be isolated and even produced in the laboratory by chemical synthesis, we reasoned that a 10-membered ring homo-clavulyne might also be stable, accessible by synthesis, and available for efforts to develop its therapeutic potential. In fact, an appropriate orchestration of Wittig olefination, regio- and stereoselective 1,4-borylation/oxidation, Sonogashira cross-coupling, and ring-closing Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi reactions are capable of generating a homo-clavulyne enediyne but only as a fugitive intermediate on a path to the product of a premature Bergman cycloaromatization. Like the pre-clavulyne enediyne 1 that inspired it, the homo-clavulyne enediyne is elusive and too close to the margins of chemical stability. Despite the unexpected result, the key strategy of Sonogashira cross-coupling, followed by intramolecular Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi reaction leading to a fleeting benzenoid diradical intermediate analogous to 2 can be applicable to the biomimetic synthesis of clavulynes themselves. This work is part of a larger, ongoing effort to design and produce clavulyne-inspired compounds with improved stability and potential utility as starting points for the development of enediynes or latent enediynes with genuine therapeutic value.

All reactions were performed in oven-dried or flame-dried glassware under N2 by standard Schlenk techniques with a dry N2/vacuum manifold unless otherwise indicated. CuI was purified by washing with refluxing THF in Soxhlet extractor and stored under N2. All other reagents were purchased and used as received. Molecular sieves (4 Å, beads, 8–12 mesh) were activated in vacuum oven overnight before using. All solvents used were HPLC grade and dried by running through activated alumina columns or from Sure/Seal™ or AcroSeal™ bottles. Where indicated as strictly deoxygenated, THF was freshly distilled from sodium/benzophenone before use. Reactions were monitored via analytical thin-layer chromatography (TLC) conducted on Merck Silica gel 60 F254 plates containing a fluorescent indicator, which were visualized with iodine, ceric ammonium molybdate, KMnO4, p-anisaldehyde stain and/or UV light. Compounds were purified by flash column chromatography on Silicycle SiliaFlash P60 (230–400 mesh) silica gel or preparative TLC on SiliaPlate™ (20 × 20 cm, 1000 μm) containing a fluorescent indicator with ACS grade solvents. Where used, Celite filtering agent was Celite 545 purchased from Thermo Scientific. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were obtained on 500 MHz Bruker spectrometers at 22 °C. 1H and 13C spectra were referenced to residual solvent (CDCl3: δ 7.26 ppm for 1H NMR and δ 77.16 ppm for 13C NMR). The multiplicities are abbreviated as follows: s = singlet, d = doublet, t = triplet, q = quartet, p = pentet, dd = doublet of doublets, ddd = doublet of doublet of doublets, dddd = doublet of doublet of doublet of doublets, dtt = doublet of triplet of triplets, td = triplet of doublets, tdd = triplet of doublet of doublets, qd = quartet of doublets, m = multiplet, and br = broad signal. Coupling constants were measured in Hz and abbreviated as J. Infrared (IR) spectra were recorded on a Nicolet 6700 FT-IR equipped with a 30,000–200 cm−1 diamond. High-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) data were obtained on an Agilent 6230 LC/TOF with liquid chromatography electrospray ionization (ESI).

### Procedures

#### Iodide 9

To a 500-mL round-bottom flask charged with a magnetic stir bar was added 8 (5 g, 32.43 mmol, 1 equiv), iodine (16.46 g, 64.87 mmol, 2 equiv), and CH2Cl2 (162 mL, 0.2 M). The solution was cooled to 0 °C and added pyridine (3.92 mL, 48.65 mmol, 1.5 equiv) slowly, then stirred for 16 h at room temperature. The reaction was quenched with 10% aq. ascorbic acid solution (150 mL). The organic layer was separated, and the aqueous layer was extracted with CH2Cl2 (80 mL × 3). The combined organic layers were dried over anhydrous MgSO4 and filtered, then concentrated in vacuo. The crude residue was purified via flash chromatography (0–15 % EtOAc/hexanes) to afford iodide 9 (7.80 g, 86%) as a white solid.

TLC Rf = 0.36 (20% EtOAc/hexanes); all characterizations matched with previously reported literature.29
